blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — OTC diphenhydramine sedation precautions
stem: A client plans to take OTC diphenhydramine for allergy symptoms. Which teaching is most important?

options.A: Marked drowsiness may occur; avoid alcoholic beverages and use caution with driving or operating machinery after taking a dose.
options.B: Mild drowsiness is expected to resolve with activity, so driving is acceptable after the first dose if allergy symptoms improve.
options.C: Alcohol can be used with diphenhydramine at bedtime because it reduces the medication-related drowsiness the next morning.
options.D: Sedatives or tranquilizers can be combined routinely with diphenhydramine because they lessen its central nervous system effects.

rationale: Current OTC diphenhydramine Drug Facts labeling states that marked drowsiness may occur, instructs users to avoid alcoholic beverages, warns that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness, and advises caution when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery. Therefore A accurately summarizes the principal sedation-related safety teaching. B, C, and D incorrectly portray driving, alcohol, or other sedating drugs as safe or protective despite the label warnings.
educational_objective: Teach clients that OTC diphenhydramine can cause marked drowsiness, that alcohol and other sedating drugs can intensify this effect, and that driving or operating machinery requires caution.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / FDA OTC labeling
source_version_date: DailyMed Drug Facts updated August 4, 2026; accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Warnings — Ask a doctor or pharmacist before use; When using this product.
source_claim_supported: Diphenhydramine may cause marked drowsiness; alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness; alcoholic beverages should be avoided; caution is advised when driving or operating machinery.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: educate client about medications; evaluate client response to medication; administer medications safely.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as substantive sedation-related counseling statements of comparable length.
Used a current August 2026 OTC Drug Facts label and retained a single accurately labeled safety statement.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A is uniquely correct; all options are closely length-matched, and B–D directly conflict with current OTC sedation warnings rather than serving as implausible filler.
